strengths: Provides a rigorous, end-to-end theoretical characterization of RLVR training dynamics on a compositional reasoning task, including polynomial-time convergence guarantees for short-horizon learning, an exponentially flat gradient barrier beyond a critical horizon, and precise characterizations of grokking-like vs. relay dynamics under mixed-difficulty training depending on the difficulty ratio R.

The introduction of Fourier/harmonic analysis on finite non-abelian groups to handle trajectory-level conditioning in long-horizon compositional RL is a genuinely novel technical tool that cleanly separates target, in-context distractor, and vocabulary distractor contributions to the policy gradient, enabling tractable analysis of posterior-vs-prior gaps that would otherwise require combinatorial trajectory enumeration.

The theoretical results connect coherently to and help explain existing empirical phenomena in the RLVR literature (edge-of-competence effects, grokking/aha-moments, curriculum learning), offering a plausible optimization-based mechanism (implicit curriculum via gradient relay) for why outcome-only rewards can still drive long-horizon learning.

The paper is unusually thorough for a theory contribution, with detailed proof overviews in the main text and an extensive, carefully organized appendix that traces the induction arguments needed to control attention scores and posterior probabilities across the whole training trajectory.

Synthetic experiments qualitatively corroborate the two predicted regimes (relay under moderate R vs. prolonged plateau under large R) as well as the short-horizon vs. long-horizon fixed-length reward/attention dynamics, providing some empirical grounding for the theory.
Limitations are stated honestly and specifically (single axis of difficulty variation, abstracted setting, no coverage of planning/search reasoning patterns).
weaknesses: The theoretical setting is highly idealized: a single attention layer with a hand-constructed, frozen MLP that perfectly implements atomic one-step transitions, zero initialization of Q, and orthonormal embeddings. While this isolates the attention/composition mechanism cleanly, it is far from how RLVR operates on real, jointly-trained multi-layer LLMs, so the extent to which the identified mechanisms (relay vs. grokking) transfer to practical RLVR training is unclear.

There is a notable mismatch between theory and experiments: the theory crucially assumes G is a finite non-abelian simple group (to avoid commutative shortcuts, Remark 3.1), but the experiments use an abelian cyclic group Z_96 'for experimental convenience,' with only a brief, unquantified claim that shortcut effects are 'mild' for the lengths considered—this is not rigorously justified.

Experimental validation is limited to a single small synthetic setup (one group, a handful of length configurations, two R values), with no real-world or larger-scale/LLM experiments, no quantitative comparison to theoretical rates (e.g., predicted plateau lengths vs. observed), and no ablations testing sensitivity to the many structural assumptions.

The gradient/posterior characterizations (e.g., Lemma 6.2, Proposition B.2) require delicate scaling conditions on step-invariant probabilities (e.g., L^2 δ_L/Δ_L = o(1)(1-Δ_L), p_{L,2}/p_{L,1} = o(1)(1-Δ_L)) that must be verified to hold throughout the entire training trajectory via nested inductions; while the appendix does this, the overall argument is intricate and the reader must trust a long chain of interlocking lemmas without independent numerical validation of intermediate quantities.

The main text's treatment of the difficulty-ratio regimes is somewhat coarse (ω(1) vs O(1) for R), and the paper does not explore or characterize intermediate/mixed regimes, nor does it give matching lower bounds establishing tightness beyond the specific asymptotic scalings analyzed.

Presentation is extremely dense with heavy notation and many assumptions/constants (CB, cx, ϵ, σ0, etc.), which, combined with the reliance on a lengthy 37-page appendix for essentially all rigor, may limit accessibility and independent verifiability by readers outside this specific theoretical tradition.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel technical tool -- Fourier/representation-theoretic analysis on finite (non-abelian simple) groups -- to make trajectory-level, long-horizon policy-gradient conditioning tractable; this seems to be a non-trivial and reusable contribution to the theory-of-RL-for-LLMs literature.

Provides end-to-end, non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for REINFORCE-trained transformers on a compositional reasoning task, which is rare in this literature (most prior work is either purely empirical or gives only asymptotic/gradient-flow guarantees).

The 'implicit curriculum' / relay-vs-grokking dichotomy is a clean, intuitively appealing conceptual story that connects cleanly to several empirical phenomena reported elsewhere (edge-of-competence effects, RL 'aha moments', grokking in RL).

The paper is unusually thorough in relating its theoretical claims to a broad swath of recent empirical and theoretical RLVR literature, carefully delineating its contribution from closely related theory papers.
The internal logical structure (induction hypotheses, gradient lemmas, posterior-deviation estimates via spectral decomposition) is carried out carefully and the appendix gives full proofs.
weaknesses: The theoretical setting is highly stylized and far from realistic RLVR: single attention layer/head, MLP frozen to implement a hand-crafted 'perfect' atomic skill with an engineered margin structure (Eq. 7), zero initialization, and a specific orthonormal embedding scheme. It is unclear how much of the qualitative story (relay vs. grokking) survives when these idealizations are relaxed (multi-layer, multi-head, jointly-trained MLP, realistic embeddings).

The experiments use an abelian cyclic group Z_96, while the entire theory explicitly requires a non-abelian simple group (Assumption 3.1, Remark 3.1) to rule out shortcut solutions; the justification that 'commutativity-induced shortcut effects are mild' for L>=5 is asserted without rigorous or even quantitative support, which weakens the claimed empirical validation of the theory.

All empirical validation is on small synthetic tasks with a toy one-layer detached-attention model; there is no experiment on a real transformer or any natural language/math RLVR benchmark, so the practical relevance of the 'implicit curriculum' mechanism to actual LLM RLVR training remains speculative rather than demonstrated.

The results depend on a large number of fine-grained technical conditions (margin/probability ratio conditions in Lemma 6.2/Proposition B.2, constraints like c_x < (C_B-2)/(C_B+2), 'sufficiently large' C_B, various o(1)/Omega(1) regimes) whose practical scope and tightness are hard to assess, and which are not discussed intuitively in the main text, limiting accessibility and making it hard to judge how restrictive the theory actually is.

The difficulty spectrum is modeled by a single scalar knob (geometric ratio R) controlling horizon length only; real curricula differ along many axes (skill composition, semantic diversity, distributional shift), a limitation the authors acknowledge but which substantially limits the generality of the main conclusions.

No ablations isolating which modeling choices (frozen vs. trained MLP, single vs. multi-head, non-abelian vs. abelian group, zero vs. random initialization) are responsible for the predicted phenomena, making it difficult to assess robustness of the theory's predictions.

Given the density of notation and the very long appendix (57+ pages), the paper's accessibility and presentation could be substantially improved; central claims in the main text (e.g., Lemma 6.2) are stated only loosely with precise versions deferred to the appendix, making independent verification difficult within the main paper.

strengths: Tackles a timely and important open question (why outcome-only RLVR works on long-horizon compositional tasks) with rigorous end-to-end theory rather than speculation.

Introduces a genuinely novel technical toolkit — Fourier/representation-theoretic analysis on non-abelian finite groups — to make trajectory-level conditioning in long-horizon policy-gradient RL tractable, yielding sharp closed-form gradient characterizations.

The grokking-vs-relay dichotomy governed by the difficulty ratio R is a clean, falsifiable, and intuitive explanation that unifies several previously disjoint empirical observations (edge-of-competence effects, grokking/aha-moments, curriculum benefits).

Theoretical predictions (critical horizon barrier, SFT vs RL gap, plateau lengths, attention concentration) are explicitly matched against synthetic experiments showing qualitatively consistent behavior.
Extensive, carefully organized appendix with internally consistent derivations (step-invariant reductions, posterior deviation bounds, spectral decay controls) and clear proof signposting.
Comprehensive related-work positioning relative to both empirical RLVR studies and prior transformer-RL theory.
weaknesses: Strong simplifying assumptions (frozen hand-crafted MLP implementing atomic skills, single-layer detached attention, orthogonal positional embeddings, non-abelian simply-transitive group structure) create a substantial gap between the theoretical model and real transformers/LLMs, limiting confidence in direct transfer of conclusions.

The synthetic experiments use an abelian cyclic group, which contradicts the non-abelian assumption central to the theory (used to suppress shortcut/path-collision effects); the claim that this discrepancy is 'mild' for L≥5 is asserted rather than empirically substantiated.

Experimental validation is limited to a single synthetic setup with few (R, L) configurations and only qualitative trend-matching, without quantitative comparison to predicted plateau lengths/convergence rates.
No validation on real or even small-scale LLM RLVR setups, leaving the connection between the abstracted state-tracking task and practical RLVR somewhat speculative.

Restrictive regimes and constants (CB = O(1), bounds on R and c_x) are mathematically necessary but their practical interpretability (e.g., how 'difficulty ratio' maps to real curricula) is not discussed in depth.

strengths: Tackles an important, timely open question about mechanisms of RLVR on compositional reasoning with a rigorous theoretical approach rather than pure speculation.
The Fourier analysis on finite groups is a novel and elegant technical tool that converts intractable trajectory-level conditioning into tractable spectral calculations.

Theory yields sharp, falsifiable predictions (grokking vs relay regimes governed by difficulty ratio R) that are tested in both controlled synthetic settings and real LLM RLVR experiments (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen3-4B on N-digit multiplication).
Clean short-horizon vs long-horizon RL/SFT comparison gives a concrete mechanistic explanation (exponentially flat gradient region) for a widely observed empirical phenomenon.
Assumptions are stated explicitly and proofs are detailed in the appendix, aiding scrutiny and reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
Limitations are honestly and specifically discussed rather than glossed over.
weaknesses: The theoretical model relies on many simplifying assumptions (frozen perfectly-pretrained MLP, orthogonal embeddings, decoupled attention scores, non-abelian simply transitive group, near-zero init) that abstract away much of the difficulty of real transformer RLVR, raising doubts about transferability of the mechanism.

Synthetic experiments use an abelian cyclic group, contradicting the non-abelian assumption required for the theory's collision-sparsity condition, with only a brief informal justification that this is acceptable.

Real-model LLM experiments are largely qualitative/visual pattern-matching to 'relay' vs 'grokking' curves rather than quantitative tests of the specific rates/exponents predicted by the theorems, leaving the theory-practice link mostly illustrative.

Derived convergence rates depend on model-specific constants (C_B, d, c_x) with no clear empirical analogue in real transformers, making the quantitative predictions essentially unverifiable in practice.

The central qualitative dichotomy (large-gap grokking vs small-gap relay) is intuitive given prior curriculum-learning and RL-grokking literature; the primary novelty is the rigorous derivation rather than the phenomenon itself, and framing as 'first end-to-end' analysis could be tempered.
Dense, proof-heavy presentation with heavy reliance on appendix material and substantial notational overhead may limit accessibility.

Only the attention module is trained while the MLP is frozen/hand-constructed, which is far from practical end-to-end fine-tuning; the paper does not discuss how joint training might alter the derived thresholds or curriculum dynamics.

strengths: Provides a genuinely novel technical toolkit (Fourier/harmonic analysis on finite groups applied to policy-gradient dynamics) for analyzing long-horizon, outcome-only RL, which seems to be a new contribution to the theory-of-RLVR literature and could be reused by future work.

The theory yields concrete, falsifiable, quantitative predictions (critical horizon/flat-gradient barrier for RL vs. SFT, grokking-style plateaus under large difficulty ratio R, relay dynamics under moderate R, explicit plateau-length and mastery-time formulas) rather than only qualitative claims.

The paper goes beyond pure theory and tests its predictions in two separate empirical settings: a controlled synthetic group-action task that mirrors the theoretical assumptions, and real RLVR runs with GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen3-4B-Base on N-digit multiplication. The qualitative match (smooth easy-to-hard progression vs. prolonged plateaus with large digit gaps) across both settings strengthens the paper's central claim.

The proof is carefully organized (step-invariant probability reduction, posterior deviation via group Fourier transforms, induction-based tracking of two scalar attention parameters q,r) and the appendix provides full derivations, which aids reproducibility of the theoretical results.

The paper situates itself clearly relative to prior empirical (edge-of-competence, grokking, entropy-mechanism) and theoretical (outcome-based RL convergence, curriculum RL) literature, and explains conceptually why RLVR works despite sparse terminal rewards.
weaknesses: The theoretical model relies on strong simplifying assumptions that are quite far from practical LLMs: a single attention layer, an MLP that is frozen and already perfectly implements the atomic one-step operation (Assumption 3.4, with very specific margin structure in Eq. 8), zero initialization of Q, and orthonormal token embeddings. This essentially assumes away the hardest part of reasoning (acquiring atomic skills) and reduces the problem to learning an attention-based permutation/retrieval task, which may limit how much the results explain real multi-step reasoning capability acquisition in LLMs.

The compositional reasoning task (simply-transitive non-abelian group action with bounded collision sparsity, Assumptions 3.1-3.2) is a stylized abstraction of "reasoning," and the paper does not clearly establish how representative this setting is of more realistic reasoning structures (e.g., math word problems, multi-hop QA) beyond the N-digit multiplication analogy, which is not literally an instance of the formal group-composition model.

The synthetic experiments deliberately use an abelian cyclic group (Z_96) "for experimental convenience," which directly violates Assumption 3.1 (non-abelian simple group) underlying the theory; while the authors argue commutativity effects are mild for the lengths tested, this is a notable mismatch between the theoretical setup and its own synthetic validation.

The connection between the formal theory and the real-model LLM experiments (N-digit multiplication with Qwen models) is only qualitative/analogical—the real experiments validate the high-level narrative (implicit curriculum, relay vs. grokking) but not any of the paper's precise quantitative predictions (e.g., exact plateau-length scaling in d, CB, R), so the empirical support for the specific theorems is indirect.

The real-model validation is limited to a single task family (integer multiplication) and two model scales, which constrains the generality of the empirical claims; it is unclear whether the smooth-vs-large-gap dichotomy transfers to more semantically rich reasoning domains (math, code, multi-hop reasoning) where difficulty is not a simple scalar like digit count.

The paper is extremely dense and relies on a large number of nested assumptions, constants (CB, cx, σ0, B, etc.), and asymptotic regimes (d → ∞), which makes it hard for readers to assess the tightness/practical relevance of the bounds or to independently verify correctness without substantial effort; the core text defers almost all rigor to a ~40-page appendix.

The qualitative finding that very large difficulty gaps cause delayed/grokking-like progress while smooth gaps enable relay is somewhat expected a priori from a curriculum-learning perspective; the paper's main novel value added is the precise mechanistic/quantitative characterization, but this makes the significance of the contribution partly incremental relative to existing curriculum-learning and grokking literature (e.g., Sun et al. 2025; Bu et al. 2025) that already discuses similar phenomena, albeit less formally.

strengths: First end-to-end convergence analysis of outcome-based RL (REINFORCE) training a transformer on compositional reasoning, with explicit, non-asymptotic iteration complexity guarantees, going beyond prior static-data or asymptotic results.

Introduces a novel and elegant technical tool: Fourier analysis on finite (non-abelian) groups to handle L-fold convolutions of trajectory measures, making long-horizon posterior/gradient estimation tractable.

Provides a clear, unifying conceptual narrative (relay vs. grokking regimes governed by the difficulty ratio R) that connects and explains disparate empirical phenomena in the RLVR literature (plateaus, 'aha moments', edge-of-competence effects).

Validates predictions at multiple levels of fidelity: synthetic experiments matching the theoretical setup, and real LLM RLVR experiments (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen3-4B) on N-digit multiplication, showing consistent qualitative agreement.

Extensive and carefully structured appendix with detailed proofs (gradient characterization, spectral decomposition, posterior estimation, induction arguments for both regimes) supporting reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The theoretical model relies on strong simplifications (single-layer, single-head attention; frozen hand-constructed MLP implementing atomic skills exactly; position-only attention scores; orthogonal positional embeddings) that are far from practical transformers, creating a sizable gap to the real-model experiments.

The synthetic experiments use an abelian cyclic group, which technically violates the core non-abelian simple group assumption (Assumption 3.1) underlying the Fourier-analytic machinery; the justification that collision effects are 'mild' is not quantitatively substantiated.

The real-model N-digit multiplication task is only loosely analogous to the formal group-composition/state-tracking task, so those experiments serve as qualitative corroboration rather than a direct empirical test of the theorems.

The notion of 'difficulty' is restricted to sequence length/horizon, excluding other realistic axes (skill rarity, semantic context shifts, planning/search), which the authors acknowledge but which limits the generality of the 'difficulty spectrum' claims.
The paper is dense and notation-heavy with many interdependent regimes and lemmas, making independent verification difficult without substantial effort through the ~40-page appendix.

Synthetic validation is relatively limited in scope (few horizon/ratio combinations), without a systematic quantitative sweep confirming the predicted scaling rates (e.g., plateau length vs. d, R, C_B).
